title: Sound Before Script

learn.summary: Adults who skip pronunciation early pay for it forever: you cannot reliably remember, or even hear, words whose sounds your brain lumps together. Spend your first weeks mapping the language's phoneme inventory — the specific set of sounds it distinguishes — before drilling vocabulary. Your ears train faster than your mouth, so prioritize discrimination (hearing differences) first.

do: List the 5-10 sounds in your target language that do not exist in your native language, with an example word for each.

children.title: Phoneme Inventory

learn.summary: Every language selects a subset of possible human sounds: Spanish has 5 vowels, English roughly 12-14 (dialect-dependent), Danish over 20. The dangerous sounds are not the exotic ones but the near-misses — Japanese lacks the English l/r contrast, Arabic distinguishes emphatic consonants English speakers merge. Study the inventory as a checklist so you know exactly which contrasts need deliberate training.

do: Find the Wikipedia phonology article for your target language and mark every sound absent from your native language.

children.title: Minimal Pairs

learn.summary: A minimal pair is two words differing by a single sound — ship/sheep, Korean 불/뿔. Minimal-pair drills, where you hear a word and must pick which of two you heard, are the fastest known way to build new sound categories in an adult brain; perception research shows measurable gains within a few hundred trials with immediate feedback. Train the pairs your native language merges.

do: Do 10 minutes of minimal-pair listening drills on 3 days this week, focusing on your two hardest contrasts.

children.title: IPA Basics

learn.summary: The International Phonetic Alphabet gives every human speech sound one unambiguous symbol, which frees you from misleading spellings — French 'eau' is just /o/. You do not need the whole chart; learning the 30-40 symbols relevant to your language pair takes an afternoon and pays off every time you open a dictionary. It also gives you vocabulary for what your mouth is doing: voicing, aspiration, nasal vowels.

do: Learn the IPA symbols for every phoneme in your target language and transcribe 10 words you already know.

children.title: Prosody & Rhythm

learn.summary: Prosody — stress, rhythm, intonation, and (in languages like Mandarin, Vietnamese, or Swedish) tone or pitch accent — carries more of your 'accent' than individual consonants do. Listeners forgive a wrong vowel far more readily than wrong sentence melody. Hum sentences without words to isolate the tune; it feels silly and works remarkably well.

do: Pick 5 recorded sentences, hum their melody without words, then say them mimicking the exact pitch contour.
